item.title: (1.1) Vector Algebra
item.description:
1.1 Vector Algebra#

A scalar has only a size (temperature, mass, charge). A vector has a size and a direction (velocity, force, electric field). Strictly, a vector is not just “three numbers”: it is three numbers that change in a particular way when you rotate your axes. The last part of this section explains what that means.

Vector operations#

You add vectors component by component; the order doesn't matter. Picture it as placing arrows head to tail. Subtracting \( \vec{B} \) means adding \( \vec{B} \) reversed. Multiplying by a scalar \( a \) stretches the arrow by \( a \) without turning it (it flips round if \( a < 0 \)).

item.title: (1.2) Differential Calculus
item.description:
1.2 Differential Calculus#

An ordinary derivative \( df/dx \) tells you how fast \( f \) changes as you move along a line.

In three dimensions one number is not enough, because the rate of change depends on which direction you move. The fix is the “del” operator:

item.title: (1.3) Integral Calculus
item.description:
1.3 Integral Calculus#

Line, surface and volume integrals#

Line integral of a vector field along a path from \( a \) to \( b \):

\[\int_a^b \vec{v} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}}\]

At each small step along the path, take the part of \( \vec{v} \) that points along the step, and add them all up. The work done by a force is the classic example. Usually the answer depends on which path you take, not just on where you start and finish. Around a closed loop it is written \( \oint \vec{v} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}} \); going round the other way flips the sign.

item.title: (1.4) Curvilinear Coordinates
item.description:
1.4 Curvilinear Coordinates#

Choosing coordinates that match the shape of the problem saves a lot of work. A charged ball is a nightmare in \( x, y, z \) and easy in spherical coordinates. Two systems cover almost everything in this course.

Spherical coordinates#

\( (r, \theta, \phi) \):

  • \( r \) is the distance from the origin (\( r \geq 0 \));
  • \( \theta \) is the angle down from the \( z \)-axis, like latitude measured from the North Pole (\( 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi \));
  • \( \phi \) is the angle round from the \( x \)-axis, like longitude (\( 0 \leq \phi < 2\pi \)).
\[x = r\sin\theta\cos\phi, \qquad y = r\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = r\cos\theta\]

The three unit vectors are mutually perpendicular and right-handed, \( \vu{r} \cross \vu{\theta} = \vu{\phi} \). In Cartesian terms,

item.title: (1.5) The Dirac Delta Function
item.description:
1.5 The Dirac Delta Function#

A puzzle: the divergence of \( \vu{r}/r^2 \)#

The field \( \vec{v} = \vu{r}/r^2 \) (the shape of a point charge's field) causes a problem. Its divergence, worked out in spherical coordinates, is

\[\div{\vec{v}} = \frac{1}{r^2}\pdv{}{r}\left( r^2 \cdot \frac{1}{r^2} \right) = \frac{1}{r^2}\pdv{}{r}(1) = 0\]

That is zero everywhere the formula makes sense. But the flux through a sphere of radius \( R \) around the origin is

item.title: (1.6) The Theory of Vector Fields
item.description:
1.6 The Theory of Vector Fields#

The Helmholtz theorem#

If you know a vector field's divergence and its curl everywhere, you know the field — as long as it dies away fast enough far from its sources.

This explains the shape of the whole subject. Maxwell's equations don't tell you \( \vec{E} \) and \( \vec{B} \) directly. They tell you the divergence and the curl of each. Two fields, each needing a divergence and a curl: that is why there are four equations.

item.title: (2.1) The Electric Field
item.description:
2.1 The Electric Field#

The basic question#

Electrodynamics asks one question: given some charges (the source charges), what force do they exert on another charge \( Q \) (the test charge)? The answer is given using fields. The source charges don't reach out and push \( Q \) directly. Instead they set up an electric field filling all of space, and \( Q \) feels whatever field there is at its own position.

item.title: (2.2) Divergence and Curl of Electrostatic Fields
item.description:
2.2 Divergence and Curl of Electrostatic Fields#

The Helmholtz theorem (§1.6) says a field is fixed once you know its divergence and its curl. This section finds both for \( \vec{E} \).

Field lines and flux#

Field lines are drawn so that at every point they run along \( \vec{E} \), and they are packed closer together where the field is stronger. They start on positive charges and end on negative ones. They never cross, because the field can only point one way at any point.

item.title: (2.3) Electric Potential
item.description:
2.3 Electric Potential#

Definition#

Since \( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \), the line integral of \( \vec{E} \) doesn't depend on the path, and so we can define a scalar potential:

\[V(\vec{r}) \equiv -\int_{\mathcal{O}}^{\vec{r}} \vec{E} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}}\]

Here \( \mathcal{O} \) is a reference point where \( V = 0 \), usually taken at infinity. The difference in potential between two points,

\[V(\vec{b}) - V(\vec{a}) = -\int_{\vec{a}}^{\vec{b}} \vec{E} \cdot \dd{\vec{l}}\]

doesn't depend on where you put the reference point. Going the other way, the gradient theorem gives

item.title: (2.4) Work and Energy in Electrostatics
item.description:
2.4 Work and Energy in Electrostatics#

Work to move a charge#

To move a test charge \( Q \) slowly from \( a \) to \( b \), you must push against the electric force. The work you do is

\[W = -Q\int_a^b \vec{E}\cdot\dd{\vec{l}} = Q\left[ V(b) - V(a) \right]\]

and it's the same for every path, because \( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \). To bring a charge in from infinity, where \( V(\infty) = 0 \),

item.title: (2.5) Conductors
item.description:
2.5 Conductors#

Basic properties#

A conductor (such as a metal) has charges that are free to move around. Treat the supply as unlimited. Five properties follow, and they all come from the first.

1. \( \vec{E} = \vec{0} \) inside. If there were a field inside, it would push the free charges. They would keep moving until their new arrangement cancelled the field. Once everything has settled, no field is left.

item.title: (3.1) Laplace's Equation
item.description:
3.1 Laplace's Equation#

The problem#

To find \( V \) by integrating over the charge, you need to know where the charge is. Usually you don't. On a conductor, the charge moves around in response to everything nearby, so where it ends up is part of the answer, not part of the question.

So instead we solve the differential equation directly. Where there is no charge, Poisson's equation becomes Laplace's equation:

item.title: (3.2) The Method of Images
item.description:
3.2 The Method of Images#

The idea#

The uniqueness theorem (§3.1) says any method of finding a solution is fine. If your potential satisfies Poisson's equation in the region you care about, and matches the boundary conditions, it is the right answer.

The method of images uses this. You remove the awkward conductor and replace it with a pretend charge, the image charge, placed where it gives the right boundary condition. The image isn't real. It is a trick that produces the correct potential in the region you care about. It must sit outside that region, so it doesn't change the charge inside.

item.title: (3.S) Green's Functions
item.description:
3.S Green's Functions#

Supplement: beyond Griffiths, but built on him. Read it after §3.1–3.2. It uses Griffiths' SI units and notation throughout (\( \gr \), \( \mathscr{V} \), \( \mathscr{S} \), \( \dd{\tau} \), \( \dd{\vec{a}} \)), and every step points back to the equation in Griffiths it comes from (5th edition numbering). The only new idea is the Green's function \( G \) itself. For further reading: Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics, §1.8–1.10, and Zangwill, Modern Electrodynamics, §8.4–8.5. Jackson uses Gaussian units, so his \( G \) is \( 4\pi\epsilon_0 \) times ours.

item.title: (3.3) Separation of Variables
item.description:
3.3 Separation of Variables#

The method#

Separation of variables is the standard way to solve Laplace's equation when the boundaries lie along coordinate lines or surfaces (flat plates for \( x, y, z \), spheres for \( r, \theta, \phi \)). You guess that the potential is a product of functions that each depend on only one variable:

\[V(x,y) = X(x)Y(y)\]

This turns one hard partial differential equation into two easy ordinary ones. The guess looks too restrictive, since most functions are not products like this. But you can add up as many product solutions as you like, and sums of them can match any boundary condition. The uniqueness theorem then guarantees the answer is right.

item.title: (3.4) Multipole Expansion
item.description:
3.4 Multipole Expansion#

Approximate potentials far away#

From far enough away, any small blob of charge looks like a point charge. The multipole expansion turns that into a precise series: a point-charge term, then smaller and smaller corrections in powers of \( 1/r \).

Start from \( V = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \rho(\vec{r'})/\gr, \dd{\tau'} \). With \( \alpha \) the angle between \( \vec{r} \) and \( \vec{r'} \), the cosine rule gives

item.title: (4.1) Polarization
item.description:
4.1 Polarization#

Dielectrics#

Chapters 2 and 3 were about conductors, where charge moves freely. This chapter is about dielectrics: insulators such as glass, plastic or water, where every electron stays attached to its own atom. These bound charges can't travel through the material. But they can shift a tiny bit inside each atom or molecule, and those tiny shifts are enough to change the field a lot.

This happens in two ways.

item.title: (4.2) The Field of a Polarized Object
item.description:
4.2 The Field of a Polarized Object#

Bound charges#

If you know the polarization \( \vec{P} \), you can find the potential by adding up the potentials of all the tiny dipoles:

\[V(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int_V \frac{\vec{P}(\vec{r'})\cdot\vu{\gr}}{\gr^2}\dd{\tau'}\]

Using \( \grad'(1/\gr) = \vu{\gr}/\gr^2 \) and integrating by parts turns this into two terms, each with a clear meaning:

item.title: (4.3) The Electric Displacement
item.description:
4.3 The Electric Displacement#

Gauss's law in a dielectric#

In a dielectric there are two kinds of charge. Bound charge comes from the polarization. Free charge is everything else: charge you put there on purpose and control, such as the charge on a capacitor plate.

\[\rho = \rho_b + \rho_f\]

Gauss's law counts all of it. Put in \( \rho_b = -\div{\vec{P}} \):

\[\epsilon_0 \div{\vec{E}} = \rho_f - \div{\vec{P}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \div{\left( \epsilon_0\vec{E} + \vec{P} \right)} = \rho_f\]

Now define the electric displacement

item.title: (4.4) Linear Dielectrics
item.description:
4.4 Linear Dielectrics#

Susceptibility, permittivity, dielectric constant#

In most materials, as long as the field isn't too strong, the polarization is proportional to the field:

\[\vec{P} = \epsilon_0 \chi_e \vec{E}\]

\( \chi_e \) is the electric susceptibility: a pure number that says how easily the material polarizes. Materials that behave like this are called linear dielectrics.

\( \vec{E} \) here is the total field, including the field made by the polarization itself, not just the field you applied from outside.

item.title: (5.1) The Lorentz Force Law
item.description:
5.1 The Lorentz Force Law#

Magnetic fields#

Magnetic fields are made by moving charges, and they push only on moving charges. Two parallel wires carrying current the same way attract; carrying current opposite ways, they repel. Electrostatics can't explain this, because both wires are electrically neutral. Something new is going on: magnetism.

The force law#

The magnetic force on a charge \( Q \) moving with velocity \( \vec{v} \) is

item.title: (5.2) The Biot-Savart Law
item.description:
5.2 The Biot-Savart Law#

Steady currents#

A steady current is a flow that has been going forever at the same rate and never changes. Charges are moving, but the amount of charge at each point stays the same, so \( \div{\vec{J}} = 0 \).

No real current is perfectly steady, but it's a very good approximation. Steady currents are to magnetostatics what charges at rest are to electrostatics.

The law#

The magnetic field of a steady current in a wire is

item.title: (5.3) The Divergence and Curl of B
item.description:
5.3 The Divergence and Curl of B#

The Helmholtz theorem says a field is fixed by its divergence and curl. Both can be worked out from the Biot-Savart law.

The divergence#

\[\div{\vec{B}} = 0\]

everywhere, always, not just for steady currents. This is one of Maxwell's equations. It says there are no magnetic monopoles: no isolated north or south poles. Cut a bar magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets, each with both poles. Magnetic field lines never start or stop; they always form closed loops.

item.title: (5.4) Magnetic Vector Potential
item.description:
5.4 Magnetic Vector Potential#

The vector potential#

\( \div{\vec{B}} = 0 \) always, so by §1.6 we can write \( \vec{B} \) as the curl of something:

\[\vec{B} = \curl{\vec{A}}\]

\( \vec{A} \) is the magnetic vector potential. It plays the role that \( V \) plays for \( \vec{E} = -\grad V \). The saving is smaller, though: \( V \) replaced three components with one number, but \( \vec{A} \) still has three components.

item.title: (6.1) Magnetization
item.description:
6.1 Magnetization#

Three kinds of magnetic material#

Every material responds a little to a magnetic field by becoming magnetized. There are three types of response:

  • Paramagnets (e.g. aluminium, oxygen) become magnetized along the field, and are weakly pulled towards a magnet.
  • Diamagnets (e.g. water, copper, bismuth) become magnetized against the field, and are weakly pushed away. In fact every material is diamagnetic; it just goes unnoticed when a stronger effect is also present.
  • Ferromagnets (e.g. iron, nickel) stay magnetized after the field is removed. The effect is far stronger than the other two. This is what fridge magnets are.

In every case the cause is the tiny magnetic dipoles of atoms, which come from the electrons' orbits and from electron spin.

item.title: (6.2) The Field of a Magnetized Object
item.description:
6.2 The Field of a Magnetized Object#

Bound currents#

If you know the magnetization \( \vec{M} \), you can get the vector potential by adding up all the tiny dipoles:

\[\vec{A}(\vec{r}) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \frac{\vec{M}(\vec{r'})\cross\vu{\gr}}{\gr^2}\dd{\tau'}\]

Integrating by parts, just as in §4.2, splits this into a volume term and a surface term:

item.title: (6.3) The Auxiliary Field H
item.description:
6.3 The Auxiliary Field H#

Ampère's law in magnetized materials#

In magnetized matter there are two kinds of current. Bound current comes from the magnetization. Free current is charge actually flowing, the current you drive through wires with a battery and control:

\[\vec{J} = \vec{J}_b + \vec{J}_f\]

Ampère's law counts all of it. Put in \( \vec{J}_b = \curl{\vec{M}} \):

\[\frac{1}{\mu_0}\curl{\vec{B}} = \vec{J}_f + \curl{\vec{M}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \curl{\left( \frac{\vec{B}}{\mu_0} - \vec{M} \right)} = \vec{J}_f\]

Now define the auxiliary field

item.title: (6.4) Linear and Nonlinear Media
item.description:
6.4 Linear and Nonlinear Media#

Magnetic susceptibility and permeability#

For paramagnets and diamagnets, as long as the field isn't too strong, the magnetization is proportional to the field. By convention it's written using \( \vec{H} \), not \( \vec{B} \):

\[\vec{M} = \chi_m \vec{H}\]

\( \chi_m \) is the magnetic susceptibility, a pure number. Materials like this are called linear media.

Using \( \vec{H} \) here is a bit odd. The electric version, \( \vec{P} = \epsilon_0\chi_e\vec{E} \), uses \( \vec{E} \), not \( \vec{D} \). But the convention is too well established to change, and it makes the link between \( \vec{B} \) and \( \vec{H} \) simple:

item.title: (7.1) Electromotive Force
item.description:
7.1 Electromotive Force#

Ohm's law#

To keep a current flowing, you have to keep pushing the charges. In most materials the current density is proportional to the push (force per unit charge):

\[\vec{J} = \sigma \vec{f} = \sigma\left( \vec{E} + \vec{v}\cross\vec{B} \right)\]

\( \sigma \) is the conductivity of the material (big for copper, tiny for glass), and \( \rho = 1/\sigma \) is its resistivity. (Don't confuse these with surface charge and charge density, which use the same letters.) Usually the magnetic part is negligible, leaving

item.title: (7.2) Electromagnetic Induction
item.description:
7.2 Electromagnetic Induction#

Faraday's law#

Faraday found that an emf appears in a loop whenever the flux through it changes, and it doesn't matter how the change happens:

  1. move the loop through a steady field (motional emf, explained in §7.1 by the magnetic force on the charges);
  2. keep the loop still and move the magnet;
  3. keep everything still and change the field's strength (e.g. turn up the current in an electromagnet).

The Lorentz force explains case 1. It can't explain cases 2 and 3: the charges in the loop aren't moving, so there's no magnetic force on them. Something else is pushing the current, and the only candidate is an electric field.

item.title: (7.3) Maxwell's Equations
item.description:
7.3 Maxwell's Equations#

The problem before Maxwell#

After Faraday, the four laws were

\[\div{\vec{E}} = \frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}, \quad \div{\vec{B}} = 0, \quad \curl{\vec{E}} = -\pdv{\vec{B}}{t}, \quad \curl{\vec{B}} = \mu_0\vec{J}\]

and the last one contradicts itself. Take the divergence of both sides. The left side is always zero (the divergence of a curl is zero). The right side is \( \mu_0\div{\vec{J}} \), which by the continuity equation is \( -\mu_0\pdv{\rho}{t} \). That is only zero if charge isn't piling up anywhere, i.e. for steady currents.

item.title: (7.4) The Field of a Rotating Magnet
item.description:
7.4 The Field of a Rotating Magnet#

The question#

Take a magnet that is symmetric about an axis (a cylindrical bar magnet, or the Earth) and spin it steadily about that axis. Does its magnetic field stay still, or does it spin round with the magnet? Are the field lines dragged round as it turns?

This section is about ideas only; there are no new calculations. It's here because students ask this question all the time, and the answer is subtler than it looks.

item.title: Intermission
item.description:
Intermission#

Chapters 1 to 7 built up the laws. Everything after this uses them.

What has been established#

The complete set of Maxwell's equations,

\[\div{\vec{E}} = \frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}, \qquad \curl{\vec{E}} = -\pdv{\vec{B}}{t}\] \[\div{\vec{B}} = 0, \qquad \curl{\vec{B}} = \mu_0\vec{J} + \mu_0\epsilon_0\pdv{\vec{E}}{t}\]

together with the Lorentz force law

\[\vec{F} = q\left( \vec{E} + \vec{v}\cross\vec{B} \right)\]

and the continuity equation \( \div{\vec{J}} = -\pdv{\rho}{t} \) (which actually follows from Maxwell's equations).

That is the whole theory. Nothing new will be added. Given the charges and currents, these equations tell you the fields. Given the fields, the force law tells you how charges move.

item.title: (8.1) Charge and Energy
item.description:
8.1 Charge and Energy#

The continuity equation#

Conservation of charge isn't an extra rule: it comes out of Maxwell's equations. Take the divergence of the Ampère–Maxwell law and use Gauss's law, and you get

\[\div{\vec{J}} = -\pdv{\rho}{t}\]

This is local conservation, which says more than “the total charge stays the same”. Total conservation alone would allow charge to vanish here and instantly reappear on the Moon. The continuity equation forbids that: charge can only leave a region by flowing out through its boundary.

item.title: (8.2) Momentum
item.description:
8.2 Momentum#

Newton's third law fails#

Picture two charges, one moving along the \( x \)-axis and the other along the \( y \)-axis, both heading towards the origin. The electric forces between them are equal and opposite, as Newton's third law expects. The magnetic forces are not. Each charge's magnetic field pushes on the other, but the two pushes point in directions that don't cancel.

So Newton's third law fails for moving charges. Conservation of momentum is usually proved from the third law, so it looks as if momentum conservation fails too.

item.title: (8.3) Magnetic Forces Do No Work
item.description:
8.3 Magnetic Forces Do No Work#

The paradox#

Magnetic forces do no work: the force is always at right angles to the velocity, so \( \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v} = 0 \) (§5.1). Yet a magnetic crane in a scrapyard lifts a whole car. Something is doing work on that car. If not the magnetic field, then what?

The car is made of iron, a ferromagnet. In the crane's field it is full of lined-up atomic dipoles, and (§6.2) that magnetization acts like a current flowing round its surface. So we can model the car as a circular loop of current.

item.title: (9.1) Waves in One Dimension
item.description:
9.1 Waves in One Dimension#

The wave equation#

A wave is a disturbance that travels along while keeping its shape (think of a pulse sent down a rope). If a shape \( f(z,t) \) moves in the \( +z \) direction at speed \( v \) without changing, then at time \( t \) it's just the starting shape slid along by \( vt \):

\[f(z,t) = g(z - vt)\]

Any function of \( z - vt \) is a wave moving right; any function of \( z + vt \) is a wave moving left. Differentiate twice and both satisfy

item.title: (9.2) Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum
item.description:
9.2 Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum#

The wave equation for E and B#

In empty space (\( \rho = 0 \), \( \vec{J} = \vec{0} \)), Maxwell's equations link the two fields: a changing \( \vec{B} \) makes \( \vec{E} \), and a changing \( \vec{E} \) makes \( \vec{B} \). To separate them, take the curl of Faraday's law and put in Ampère's law (Example 7.3-b). The result:

\[\laplacian\vec{E} = \mu_0\epsilon_0 \pdv{^2\vec{E}}{t^2}, \qquad \laplacian\vec{B} = \mu_0\epsilon_0 \pdv{^2\vec{B}}{t^2}\]

Every component obeys the wave equation of §9.1, with speed

item.title: (9.3) Electromagnetic Waves in Matter
item.description:
9.3 Electromagnetic Waves in Matter#

Waves in linear materials#

Inside a linear material with no free charge or current, Maxwell's equations look just like the vacuum ones with \( \epsilon_0 \to \epsilon \) and \( \mu_0 \to \mu \). So everything in §9.2 carries over with that swap, and waves travel at

\[v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon\mu}} = \frac{c}{n}\]

where the index of refraction is

\[n \equiv \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon\mu}{\epsilon_0\mu_0}} \approx \sqrt{\epsilon_r}\]

The approximation works because most transparent materials are barely magnetic, \( \mu \approx \mu_0 \).

item.title: (9.4) Absorption and Dispersion
item.description:
9.4 Absorption and Dispersion#

Waves in conductors#

In a conductor there are free charges, so a wave's electric field drives a current \( \vec{J} = \sigma\vec{E} \), and the current term in Ampère's law is no longer zero. (Any free charge put inside a conductor quickly spreads to the surface, dying away with time constant \( \epsilon/\sigma \). So we can take \( \rho_f = 0 \), but the current stays.)

item.title: (9.5) Guided Waves
item.description:
9.5 Guided Waves#

Wave guides#

A wave guide is a hollow metal pipe that carries electromagnetic waves along it (used for microwaves in radar and satellite dishes). Treat the walls as perfect conductors. Then at the inside surface:

\[\vec{E}^{\parallel} = \vec{0}, \qquad B^{\perp} = 0\]

(no electric field along the wall, no magnetic field into the wall).

Trapping the wave in a pipe changes things. Inside a guide the fields are generally not purely transverse. Solving Maxwell's equations with these boundary conditions gives all the sideways field components in terms of the components along the pipe, \( E_z \) and \( B_z \), and these can't both be zero.

item.title: (10.1) The Potential Formulation
item.description:
10.1 The Potential Formulation#

Scalar and vector potentials#

In electrostatics, \( \curl{\vec{E}} = \vec{0} \) let us write \( \vec{E} = -\grad V \). Once fields change with time that no longer works. But \( \div{\vec{B}} = 0 \) is still always true, so we can still write

\[\vec{B} = \curl{\vec{A}}\]

Put this into Faraday's law:

\[\curl{\left( \vec{E} + \pdv{\vec{A}}{t} \right)} = \vec{0}\]

So it's this combination, not \( \vec{E} \) on its own, that has zero curl, and it can be written as a gradient:

item.title: (10.2) Continuous Distributions
item.description:
10.2 Continuous Distributions#

Retarded potentials#

For steady sources, the potentials were integrals over the charges and currents. When things change with time, the same integrals work, with one change: each bit of source must be taken at an earlier time, to allow for the time the news takes to travel to you at speed \( c \):

\[V(\vec{r},t) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \frac{\rho(\vec{r'},t_r)}{\gr}\dd{\tau'}, \qquad \vec{A}(\vec{r},t) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \frac{\vec{J}(\vec{r'},t_r)}{\gr}\dd{\tau'}\]

where the retarded time (“retarded” meaning delayed) is

item.title: (10.3) Point Charges
item.description:
10.3 Point Charges#

The Liénard-Wiechert potentials#

For a single point charge \( q \) moving any way at all, the retarded potentials work out to

\[V(\vec{r},t) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{qc}{\left( \gr c - \vec{\gr}\cdot\vec{v} \right)}, \qquad \vec{A}(\vec{r},t) = \frac{\vec{v}}{c^2}V(\vec{r},t)\]

Everything on the right is taken at the retarded time: the moment the charge sent out the signal that is arriving now. That time is found from

\[\left| \vec{r} - \vec{w}(t_r) \right| = c\left( t - t_r \right)\]

where \( \vec{w}(t) \) is the charge's path. In words: the distance from where the charge was to where you are equals how far light travels in the time since. A point charge (moving slower than light) always has exactly one such moment.

item.title: (11.1) Dipole Radiation
item.description:
11.1 Dipole Radiation#

What radiation is#

Radiation is energy that escapes to infinity and never comes back. The power passing through a sphere of radius \( r \) is \( \oint\vec{S}\cdot\dd{\vec{a}} \). The sphere's area grows as \( r^2 \), so for the power not to shrink to zero at huge \( r \), the Poynting vector must fall no faster than \( 1/r^2 \). Since \( \vec{S} \) is (field)², the fields must fall as \( 1/r \).

item.title: (11.2) Power Radiated by a Point Charge
item.description:
11.2 Power Radiated by a Point Charge#

The Larmor formula#

The fields of a moving point charge (§10.3) have two parts: a velocity field falling as \( 1/\gr^2 \), and an acceleration field falling as \( 1/\gr \). Only the second radiates:

\[\vec{E}_{\text{rad}} = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{\gr}{\left( \vec{\gr}\cdot\vec{u} \right)^3}\left[ \vec{\gr}\cross\left( \vec{u}\cross\vec{a} \right) \right]\]

(The velocity field does hold energy, but that energy travels along with the particle rather than escaping to infinity.)

item.title: (11.3) The Radiation Reaction
item.description:
11.3 The Radiation Reaction#

The recoil#

An accelerating charge radiates energy, and that energy has to come from somewhere. So a charged particle must respond to a push slightly differently from an uncharged particle of the same mass: its own fields push back on it. This push-back is the radiation reaction. (Think of the kick a gun gives when it fires.)

The Abraham-Lorentz formula#

A first guess: set the work done by the reaction force equal to the radiated power. But that's not true moment by moment. The radiated power was worked out on a sphere at infinity, where the velocity field doesn't reach. Near the particle, though, the velocity field does hold energy, and that energy swaps back and forth between particle and field, separately from the radiation that escapes.

item.title: (12.1) The Special Theory of Relativity
item.description:
12.1 The Special Theory of Relativity#

Einstein's postulates#

In ordinary mechanics, the laws are the same in every inertial frame (any frame moving at constant velocity): drop a ball on a smoothly moving train and it falls just as it does on the platform. Electrodynamics seemed to break this rule. Maxwell's equations predict one particular speed, \( c \), and people assumed that meant speed relative to some medium, the “ether”. But experiments could find no ether. Einstein's answer was to take both ideas as basic starting points:

item.title: (12.2) Relativistic Mechanics
item.description:
12.2 Relativistic Mechanics#

Proper time and proper velocity#

Ordinary velocity \( \dd{\vec{l}}/\dd{t} \) is awkward in relativity. The distance is measured by the ground observer, but the particle's own clock would give a different time, so it's a mix of two viewpoints and changes in a messy way between frames. Instead, divide by the proper time \( \bar{t} \), the time on a clock carried along with the particle. That gives the proper velocity

item.title: (12.3) Relativistic Electrodynamics
item.description:
12.3 Relativistic Electrodynamics#

Magnetism as a relativistic phenomenon#

Magnetism isn't really a separate force. It is what electric forces look like when charges move and you take relativity into account.

Take a wire carrying a current: positive ions sitting still, and negative electrons drifting along, in equal amounts so the wire is neutral. A test charge moves alongside the wire. In the lab the wire is neutral, so there's no electric field, and the force on the test charge is purely magnetic.
